cf.title: Use instr_time for pg_stat_database block read/write time counters

input.subject: Use instr_time for pg_stat_database block read/write time counters

verdict_reasoning: No objection survived at levels 1a, 1b or 2. The problem is stated with a reproducible script in message #1, the change follows the instr_time practice that pg_stat_io and pgBufferUsage already use, and it adds no SQL, GUC, catalog or on-disk surface. The open point is sequencing against the planned pgBufferUsage rework, which the thread treats as separate later work.

brief.title: Use instr_time for pg_stat_database block read/write time counters
brief.problem: pg_stat_database truncates each I/O duration to microseconds before it adds the duration to blk_read_time and blk_write_time, so the totals undercount and drift from pg_stat_io. Users who compare the two views, or who run fast storage with sub-microsecond I/O, see different numbers for the same work.
brief.proposed_design: The patch changes pgStatBlockReadTime and pgStatBlockWriteTime from PgStat_Counter to instr_time, so the backend accumulates ticks and converts to microseconds only at stats flush. It removes the pgstat_count_buffer_{read|write}_time macros and makes the vacuum and analyze snapshot variables instr_time, which converts elapsed time straight to milliseconds.
user_visible_surface: pg_stat_database.blk_read_time and blk_write_time report higher totals that match pg_stat_io more closely; the column types do not change.
C API: the patch removes the pgstat_count_buffer_read_time and pgstat_count_buffer_write_time macros from pgstat.h.
C API: pgStatBlockReadTime and pgStatBlockWriteTime change type from PgStat_Counter to instr_time.
author_claims: With the patch, the pg_stat_database and pg_stat_io read/write totals almost match, where before write time differed by about 15%.
Removing the per-I/O microsecond conversion from the hot path gives about 0.5% more tps in a single-client, I/O-heavy pgbench -S run.
The on-disk stats format, catalogs and the vacuum log line format do not change (reviewer claim).
The style now matches pg_stat_io, pgBufferUsage and function stats, which already accumulate in instr_time.
brief.thread_state: Narayanan reviewed it and has no further code comments; Andres expects a measurable win but wants pg_stat_database to derive its times from pgBufferUsage later, in separate work. Lukas suggests doing that conversion after the parallel-worker double-counting fix is settled in the WAL statistics thread.
unclear: The patch prose has no documentation or release note hunk for the change in reported blk_read_time and blk_write_time values.
Nobody says whether this patch should go in before the planned pgBufferUsage-based rework or wait for it.
The benchmark is one setup on one client; the thread gives no results for many clients or other platforms.
The thread does not settle whether the snapshot pattern in vacuum and analyze misbehaves when track_io_timing changes mid-run.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: pgstat.h loses pgstat_count_buffer_{read|write}_time, and pgStatBlockReadTime and pgStatBlockWriteTime change type to instr_time.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: The header change and the step in reported blk_read_time and blk_write_time values fit a major release only.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: The planned pgBufferUsage rework would later replace the counters this patch retypes.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: The patch changes pgstat_count_io_op_time(), which runs on every timed read, write and extend.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: Should this patch go in before the planned pgBufferUsage-based rework of pg_stat_database I/O times, or wait for it?
Does the patch need a release note or documentation hunk saying that blk_read_time and blk_write_time totals rise after the upgrade?
What does the pgbench comparison show with many clients and on another platform, where the clock source differs?
Can the vacuum and analyze snapshot of pgStatBlockReadTime and pgStatBlockWriteTime report a wrong elapsed time when track_io_timing changes mid-run?

committability.owner_note: The owner would be a committer who knows the cumulative statistics code and the I/O timing path in pgstat_io.c. The three visible messages show none taking part; the brief reports comments from Andres later in the thread.
committability.liability: The owner signs for a one-time rise in reported blk_read_time and blk_write_time, a compile break for extensions that use the removed macros, and the per-I/O accounting path. The liability is small and may be short if the pgBufferUsage rework replaces these counters.
committability.author_follow_up: The authors posted v2 one day after the first review (message #3), and the CommitFest entry returned to a rebased state on 2026-10-09.

priority.reason: The patch touches five files, adds no user-visible surface, and closes a measured gap of about 15% in write time for users who run track_io_timing and compare pg_stat_database with pg_stat_io. The reported speed gain is about 0.5% in one single-client run, so the accuracy fix carries the case.

provisional_note: Without the code, nobody here could confirm that PgStat_StatDBEntry and the stats file keep microsecond PgStat_Counter values, or that every flush path converts the accumulated ticks exactly once. Only 3 of 13 messages were visible.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: s/shm_mq_iovec/struct iovec/
precedents_retrieved.summary: Replace the shm_mq module's own shm_mq_iovec struct with the standard POSIX struct iovec. The motivation was to remove a duplicate definition now that struct iovec can be used everywhere.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Heikki Linnakangas argued that the two structs belong to separate APIs and should stay separate. Reusing struct iovec could tie shm_mq to POSIX limits such as IOV_MAX, and it would stop shm_mq from adding its own fields later. The author accepted this and marked the entry returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
They serve a similar purpose,
but they belong to completely separate APIs; I think "incidental
deduplication" is the right term for that.

precedents_retrieved.title: Asynchronous and "direct" IO support for PostgreSQL
precedents_retrieved.authors: Andres Freund (andresfreund), David Rowley (davidrowley), Thomas Munro (macdice)
precedents_retrieved.summary: Andres Freund proposed an asynchronous IO (AIO) subsystem for Postgres, with several backends (worker processes, io_uring, posix AIO, Windows) and helpers for streaming reads and writes. The same work adds optional direct IO, so data moves between storage and shared buffers without the kernel page cache.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The entry died of inactivity. The patch set stopped applying in January 2022 and no rebased version followed. In May 2022 Aleksander Alekseev asked for a rebase and said a set of 39 patches was too large to review, and that it should be split. Michael Paquier marked it Returned with feedback after five months without activity.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I don't know what's the exact status here, but as there has been no
activity for the past five months, I have just marked the entry as RwF
for now.

precedents_retrieved.title: Show WAL stats on pg_stat_io
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds WAL I/O (writes, fsyncs, reads during recovery, and WAL segment initialization in a new IOCONTEXT_INIT) to the pg_stat_io view as IOOBJECT_WAL. Timings use track_wal_io_timing, and pg_stat_wal timings would come from pg_stat_io.
precedents_retrieved.objection: pg_stat_io ties op_bytes to a fixed block size per object and context, but some WAL reads, such as those by the WAL receiver, have a variable size. Reviewers did not agree whether to set op_bytes to 1, to NULL, or to add per-operation byte columns. Michael Paquier proposed to set the patch aside until WAL reads and writes, async I/O and cached reads are settled, so that the meaning of pg_stat_io does not change between releases. The author agreed, and the patch was marked Returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
IMHO, perhaps we'd better put this patch aside until we are absolutely
*sure* of what we want to achieve when it comes to WAL, and I am
afraid that this cannot happen until we're happy with the way we
handle WAL reads *and* writes, including WAL receiver or anything that
has the idea of pulling its own page callback with
XLogReaderAllocate() in the backend.

precedents_retrieved.title: Get rid of pgstat_count_backend_io_op*() functions
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch removes the pgstat_count_backend_io_op*() functions, so I/O counters are incremented once, and copies the pending I/O stats into the per-backend pending stats when the I/O stats flush. To make this work, per-backend stats must flush after the other stats kinds, first by placing PGSTAT_KIND_BACKEND last in the enum and later (v3) by flushing it outside the loop in pgstat_report_stat().
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier objected to the ordering dependency between stats kinds at flush time, which so far have been independent, and said the copy approach hurts readability. He also said there was no benchmark data to choose among inlining, static structures, copies or fewer diffs, so the picture was incomplete. Andres Freund rejected the alternative WalUsage-style diff approach as too costly. The thread ends with the author disagreeing, and the visible messages do not show a final decision.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Hmm.  I really have an issue with the ordering dependency this
introduces between stats kinds, assumed to happen inside the code.

precedents_retrieved.title: Fix Deadlock Issue in Single User Mode When IO Failure Occurs
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch fixes a hang in single-user mode when a relation read or write fails during startup recovery or a checkpoint: AbortBufferIO() at process exit waits on a buffer I/O lwlock that the process still holds. It makes sure all lwlocks are released before AbortBufferIO() runs, first by registering LWLockReleaseAll() as an exit callback and in v3 by calling it in AtProcExit_Buffers().
precedents_retrieved.objection: Amit Kapila tested the create table, insert and checkpoint repro and reported that the patch does not fix the problem. The second I/O error, raised during ShutdownXLOG() at exit, now ends in an assertion failure in UnpinBuffer() called from ReleaseAuxProcessResources. Michael Paquier reproduced the same trace and asked the author for an update, but the author did not respond, so the entry was returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I have tried to look into this patch and I don't think it fixes the
problem.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add parallel counters to pg_stat_statements
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add counters to pg_stat_statements that record how many times a statement was planned with parallelism and how many times it ran with parallel workers. A later version instead counted how often a parallel plan ran without any parallel workers.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Julien Rouhaud said the counters cannot tell why a parallel plan ran without workers: the executor disabled parallel mode (!es_use_parallel_mode, as with the JDBC client) or no workers were free. He asked for separate counters for each case and for better column names. Nobody answered this review, and Michael Paquier marked the entry Returned with feedback after the thread had been idle for a few weeks.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Both situations are different and in my opinion require
different (and specialized) counters to properly handle them.

precedents_retrieved.title: pg_stat_database update stats_reset only by pg_stat_reset
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch stops pg_stat_reset_single_table_counters and pg_stat_reset_single_function_counters from updating stats_reset in pg_stat_database, so that only a full pg_stat_reset changes it. The author wanted stats_reset to mark the point where all database-level counters, such as xact_commit, were reset.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Resetting the database timestamp on any per-object reset is intentional: the code comment and the 2011 commit message both say so, and nobody had complained since. Reviewers did not want to break an 8-year-old behaviour that monitoring may rely on. A changed stats_reset tells a monitoring tool that some counters in the database were reset, and per-object timestamps would add overhead and make queries more complex. The author agreed and withdrew the entry.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I agree with Daniel that breaking an 8-year-old behavior may not be of
the taste of folks relying on the current behavior, particularly
because we have not had complains about the current behavior being
bad.

precedents_retrieved.title: pg_dump -C Grant statement on create database
precedents_retrieved.summary: When pg_dump is run with -C (emit CREATE DATABASE), it would also emit the database-level GRANT statements (such as GRANT CREATE ON DATABASE), matching what pg_dumpall already produces. The patch makes emitting these grants subject to the existing -x (no privileges) option.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. The thread contains only the original report, a reply agreeing it is an oversight, and the patch submission; no review or objection to the patch appears, and the entry was returned with feedback about three months later.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Rename routines for write/read of pgstats file"
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Rename routines for write/read of pgstats file"
Reverted commit(s): Rename routines for write/read of pgstats file
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit ed823da1289, that has made pgstat_write_chunk() and
pgstat_read_chunk() available for public use.  These routines do not
have a symmetric API definition across reads and writes, with the write
part returning a void status, deferring an error detection once all the
stats entries have been processed with an ferror(), and the read part
returning a boolean status.

These routines are just tiny wrappers around fread() and fwrite(), and
extensions can just define they own routines instead of relying on the
same facilities as the core pgstat.c.  This commit removes their
declaration from the public headers, to reduce the confusion.
test_custom_stats is updated to use its own read/write routines.
Perhaps something better could be designed in the future; trying to do
so for v19 is not feasable during beta.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent found. [P4] covers per-backend I/O counters and was stopped over flush ordering between stats kinds, which this patch does not add. [P3] covers WAL in pg_stat_io. Message #13 points to the cumulative WAL statistics thread for a later pgBufferUsage rework, which is follow-up work and was not a prior rejection of this idea.

No SQL syntax, GUC, catalog or pg_dump surface changes. The column types stay the same. The only user-visible change is higher, more accurate blk_read_time and blk_write_time totals after a major upgrade, and that corrects an undercount. Removing the macros and retyping pgStatBlockReadTime breaks extension builds loudly, which is normal for a major release. A release note for the step change in values is a level 4 item.

The patch changes only backend-local accumulators and removes two macros. PgStat_StatDBEntry keeps PgStat_Counter microseconds, so the stats file, catalogs, WAL, replication and wire protocol do not change. The type change of pgStatBlockReadTime and pgStatBlockWriteTime in pgstat.h targets a major release only, and any extension that reads them fails to compile instead of misreading the values. Neither the on-disk stats layout nor that compile-time break could be confirmed without the code.

The patch changes how existing pg_stat_database I/O timing counters accumulate inside a backend. It adds no view, column, function, privilege or GUC, and it does not change who can read these statistics. Higher-precision totals of a database's own I/O time do not give an unprivileged user a new timing or data channel, and per-backend memory use stays the same. I see no security or privilege angle.

No maintenance or fit objection holds. The patch makes pg_stat_database accumulate I/O time in instr_time, as pg_stat_io, pgBufferUsage and function stats already do. Andres expects it to remove a conversion from the I/O hot path (message #5), and message #11 measures a small single-client gain. The later move to pgBufferUsage would replace these counters but gives the same precision, so users see no second change in values, and Andres asks for that move as separate work (message #9). Only the macro removal and the type change of pgStatBlockReadTime and pgStatBlockWriteTime touch the extension API, and a major release may change both. Neither [P3] nor [P4] fits: they dealt with view semantics changing between releases and with ordering between stats kinds at flush, and this patch introduces neither.

No existing feature gives per-database I/O times without the microsecond truncation: pg_stat_io is not per database, and pg_stat_statements is per query. The patch changes the type of an existing counter and adds no new mechanism; Andres (message #9) called the pgBufferUsage-based rework separate work, and Lukas (message #13) ties that rework to the open WAL statistics fix.

No demand objection applies. The change fixes a measured gap of about 15% in write time between pg_stat_database and pg_stat_io (message #1), costs non-users nothing, removes per-I/O work from a hot path that Andres expects to be a win (message #5), and adds no SQL, GUC or catalog surface. Whether to merge before or after the pgBufferUsage rework is a sequencing question for other angles.
